Limen

līmen — the threshold. Everything below it never reaches the model.

A decision layer between your coding agent and its model API. It answers, before the call is made, what the request does not need to carry: 43.6% fewer input tokens on measured traffic, task pass-rate held, running on your own machine at $0.

what it is

four decisions, made locally, in the time of one regex

Limen is a proxy you point your agent at. It speaks the OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini request shapes, records every decision it makes, and answers four questions before your prompt is sent: which tool specs this task cannot use, which old turns have gone stale, which file notes the graph says are irrelevant, and how much reasoning this step deserves. It is a System One layer — fast, cheap, fallible — sitting under the model rather than replacing it.

It ships with no third-party runtime dependencies, needs no account, and starts in observation: it records what it would have dropped and changes nothing until you name the slots you trust.

The four slots. None of them is on until you name it in SUBPROTO_APPLY, and each one is reversible on its own. The token column is the offline projection bench/ab.py --mock prints — what the slot could take from recorded prompt shapes, not yet what it took.
slotwhat it decidestokens it would cut% of input
tool_gatewhich tool schemas this turn cannot use, out of the ~24 that ride along in every request101,56228.3%
compactwhich old turns have gone stale — a superseded tool result, an error the agent already worked around14,8214.1%
contextwhich file notes the code graph says this task will not touch00.0%
efforthow much reasoning this step deserves — advisory: it names a tier and never rewrites the request00.0%
install

three routes, no account at any of them

from the source you just cloned

git clone https://github.com/aashish254/limen.git
cd limen
./install.sh                # puts `subproto` on PATH, no package index

into a virtualenv you already use

python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install .               # Python 3.9 or newer, zero dependencies

without installing anything

python3 -m subproto demo --slots   # replays 17 agent turns through the proxy

The package and the command are still named subproto; Limen is the project. Point your agent at it and check the machine before you believe anything else:

subproto doctor            # 6 measured checks: interpreter, data dir, port, keys, backends
subproto demo --slots      # 17 synthetic agent requests through the proxy, against the local mock
subproto report            # what those requests would have cost, and what the slots would have cut

438 tests and 157 mutants are the gate: bash run_tests.sh runs them, and CI runs that on Python 3.9 and 3.11 on Linux and macOS.

the numbers

the same traffic, with the system off and on

Every figure below comes out of a run on this machine at $0 against the in-repo mock. The corpus is 20 coding-agent tasks replayed 5 times through three arms: observe (nothing is changed), enforce (each slot spends its own budget), and compiled (one joint budget over the whole request). Where a number is a projection or has not been run, the caption says which.

The average request before anything is decided: a fifth of it is tool schemas the turn cannot use, and the task itself is a rounding error.

python3 bench/launch_stats.py --iters 5 on Darwin 27.0.0, 20 tasks × 5 repeats, commit 0f7a546.

Input tokens per task with the layer off, per-slot, and compiled, split by what the task is about. The reduction is flat across families, which is the point — it is not one kind of task paying for the others.

python3 bench/launch_stats.py --iters 5 on Darwin 27.0.0, 20 tasks × 5 repeats, commit 0f7a546.

The same three arms grouped by the size of the unmanaged request. Bigger requests do not get a proportionally bigger cut, so the saving does not live only in the outliers.

python3 bench/launch_stats.py --iters 5 on Darwin 27.0.0, 20 tasks × 5 repeats, commit 0f7a546.

The ablation's own corpus: what each slot would take off a request shaped like the ones it measures, priced in estimated input tokens. That is why it is not the number the arms above delivered.

python3 bench/ab.py --mock 24 --json, run by python3 bench/launch_stats.py --iters 5 — 30 requests, 359,259 est input tokens.

Pass-rate by family with the cut enforced. A saving that broke the task would be visible here as a missing bar, not as a footnote.

python3 bench/launch_stats.py --iters 5 on Darwin 27.0.0, 20 tasks × 5 repeats, commit 0f7a546.

Of the files a task is about, how many survive (recall), and of what survives, how many are the ones that matter (precision). Per-slot keeps recall and spends precision; the compiler moves both.

python3 bench/launch_stats.py --iters 5 on Darwin 27.0.0, 20 tasks × 5 repeats, commit 0f7a546.

Eight tasks built so the file the grader wants sits behind a run of large files it does not need — which is what a per-slot recency budget is worst at. Per-slot loses every one of them. This panel is the reason the compiler is the default story rather than a bonus arm.

python3 bench/launch_stats.py --iters 5 on Darwin 27.0.0, 20 tasks × 5 repeats, commit 0f7a546.

The real small model's measured cost per decision against the shape it has to answer in. One shape fits the budget; the one that would name every option does not, so the shipped path scores a single choice.

convaiinnovations/laya 0.3.20 on cpu, read from bench/laya_latency.json — measured against the local server, not re-run by the arms.

how to use it

the ladder, and where each rung earns its keep

1 — observe

Set the base URL and record. Nothing is rewritten, and the first page you read is subproto report: what your own traffic carries that it does not need.

2 — enforce what you trust

Name the slots, one at a time: SUBPROTO_APPLY=tool_gate. Each one is reversible, and the pass-rate gate is checked per arm, not pooled.

3 — compile

SUBPROTO_COMPILE=on spends a single budget over messages, tool specs and file notes together. Cheaper and more precise — and slower per decision, which is stated below rather than hidden.

The cached prefix is never rewritten. That is the whole reason a token-saving proxy can be worth anything: busting a provider's prompt cache costs more than the tokens it saves, so Limen only ever edits the part of the request the cache does not hold, and there is an invariant test that asserts byte equality on it.

the honest part

what it costs when it is wrong

The demo corpus is 17 requests and every one of them carries a decision. The regret harvest looks for the case where the wire disagrees with a cut — a file the slot dropped that the agent then read again — and it saw 14 evicted reads, of which 10 were wrong: the file came back on the next turn, so the cut cost 4,088 tokens of refetch instead of saving them. All 10 were enforced and none was shadow, so that is the price of a call made, not of a call observed — which is why Limen starts in observation, why each slot is reversible on its own, and why this bill sits on the page beside the saving. It works out at 588.2 regrettable drops per 1,000 requests. The mechanism still nets out at 43.6% fewer input tokens per task with the pass-rate held; the honest number is the pair, not the one that flatters it.

17 of the 17 requests that carried a decision still had their body on disk when the harvest ran, which is what lets the payback be counted rather than estimated.

python3 bench/launch_stats.py --iters 5 on Darwin 27.0.0 — 17 demo requests replayed with the slots enforcing, bodies stored, commit 0f7a546.

not measured

the claims this page does not make

Every one of these is a human action or a spend decision, and each is written into TODO.md as gated rather than checked off.
claimwhat it would take
−X% on your own traffica real agent session across ≥2 vendors, run by you. Nothing here has seen a human conversation; every number on this page comes from a seeded synthetic corpus.
the billed hero numberan approved API budget and a public 20-task SWE-bench-shaped set with a grader. The $ figures on this page are the in-repo mock's own tariff.
that a fine-tune beats the heuristiclabels. The published ablation says the real checkpoint loses by −0.083 precision on the corpus we carry, and 7 of its 10 cases have gold sets equal to the heuristic's own answer.
a shipped routing modelthe same labels, plus a training run and a weights release.
version 1.0a tag, a PyPI upload, and the launch post. The install routes above are git and pip-from-source until then.
that it works on Windows`os.getloadavg` is POSIX and ANSI handling differs, so CI runs Windows and reports it without gating on it.

Against other systems: the published comparison for a decision layer of this kind is TypeSafe AI's Jev, a hosted classifier at $0.042 per million tokens. Limen is local, Apache-2.0 and bills nothing. We have never run Jev, so this page carries no speed or accuracy multiplier against it — only the axis we can stand on: what our own traffic costs with the layer on and off.

Limen is the project; the package and the command are still subproto. Apache-2.0, 17 subcommands, no runtime dependencies, a Python 3.9 floor.
This page is generated: python3 bench/launch_stats.py --iters 5 && python3 tools/make_site.py. The numbers are not typed by hand, so they cannot drift from the run that produced them.
